title: 3-Read Friday #82: Digital Attention, Managing the Room, and Reframing Success
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #82 pairs a research question with two practice-facing pieces. Daniel Willingham asks whether school phone bans will actually fix student distraction, or whether long-term digital-technology use has already changed how students attend. Nimish Lad shares Robert Frisch's insights on "managing the room," arguing that senior leaders waste their team's time by failing to be explicit about why a meeting exists. Jo Castelino closes with a case against short-term measures of success, drawing on the Bjorks' distinction between performance and learning to argue for reframing success around durable, long-term retention. Barton's throughline connects attention, meeting culture, and classroom success as three places where surface signals mislead.
points: Willingham's piece asks the sharper question behind phone bans: not whether phones distract in the moment, but whether sustained digital-device use has structurally changed students' capacity to sustain focus at all.

Lad's central borrowed insight from Robert Frisch is that leaders should treat every meeting as requiring an explicit, stated purpose -- decision, discussion, or information-sharing -- because unnamed purpose is what causes meetings to collapse.

Castelino's piece extends the Bjorks' performance-versus-learning distinction into a caution against "lovely ticks in books" as a proxy for real learning, arguing success needs early wins without sacrificing desirable difficulty.

Across all three picks, Barton's selections share a skepticism of surface signals -- classroom compliance, meeting attendance, and quick correct answers can all look like success while masking the opposite underneath.
quotes: Daniel asks whether the recent trend in the US - and in the UK - for schools to ban mobile phones will solve the problem of reducing student distraction, or has the long-term use of digital technologies rendered many students unable to sustain their focus?
This is a post that should be mandatory reading for all senior leaders who organise meetings.
Nimish shares Robert Frisch’s core insights about being explicit and stage-setting to ensure that leaders don’t waste any of their team’s precious time.

In much the same way as the Bjorks distinguish between performance and learning, Jo warns against a focus on short-term measures of success (lots of lovely ticks in books), and instead suggests ways we can help students achieve and feel successful for the long term.
